steelman: Teams treat code review as the trust boundary for AI-generated code, but the signal review optimizes (perceived diff-level quality) is a poor predictor of the outcome that matters (runtime reliability). The evidence pairs a perception-outcome split (94 percent of leaders rate AI code higher-quality at review, yet 82 percent hit at least one production failure tied to it) with a defect-location fact (43 percent still needs manual debugging in production AFTER passing QA or staging). Because the dominant AI defect class is architectural and integration behavior that is not legible in a diff, the marginal return on making review stricter is bounded: you cannot inspect out of an artifact a failure mode the artifact does not contain. So agent debt is a verification-PLACEMENT problem. The leverage is to move the trust boundary from review to runtime, where the failing behavior is observable and where confirming a fix already costs real cycles (an average of three manual redeploys, 88 percent needing two to three).
strongest_attack: False dichotomy resting on a stat that argues the opposite. Claim c2 says 62 percent ship AI code WITHOUT line-by-line manual verification. That means review is not saturated, it is under-applied. If most teams are skipping careful review, then stricter review is untested, and the production failures could simply be the predictable result of lax review, which is exactly the review-strictness reading the thesis denies. The perception numbers compound this: 94 percent rating and 82 percent failure are population-level percentages, not paired measurements of the SAME reviewed code, so they do not statistically establish decoupling. On this reading the honest inference from the data is trite and pro-review (people who skip verification get burned), and the pivot to runtime is a non-sequitur dressed as a placement insight.
reconciliation: The thesis survives once the attack forces the sharper claim. The attack is defeated by c1 plus c3 read together: the failures are not confined to un-reviewed code. 43 percent still needs production debugging AFTER passing QA or staging, meaning code that DID clear a gate and was rated high-quality still fails at runtime. That is the paired evidence the attack said was missing, and it directly separates review-strictness from the outcome: the defect surfaces despite a passing gate. Mechanism c6 supplies the why: agent debt is unvetted architectural logic that accumulates because the review surface (a diff) does not expose integration and runtime behavior. So the claim is not that review is skipped and should be done, it is that even applied, praised review has bounded predictive power for this defect class because the failure information is absent from the reviewed artifact. That is non-trivial (it contradicts the default reflex to gate harder at review) and falsifiable (if stricter review reduced production failures proportionally, the thesis is wrong). The 62 percent stat is retained not as proof of laxity but as evidence that teams already privilege the review signal over runtime evidence, which is the behavior the thesis says is misplaced.
strengthened_argument: Review-time quality perception is a weak predictor of runtime reliability for AI-generated code, because the dominant defect class (architectural and integration behavior, what New Relic calls agent debt) is not legible in a diff and surfaces in production even after the code passes review, QA, and staging (43 percent). Therefore stricter review has bounded marginal return, and agent debt is a verification-PLACEMENT problem: move the trust boundary from review to runtime, where the failing behavior is observable and where confirming a fix already consumes measurable cycles. The claim explicitly does NOT depend on teams reviewing badly; the 62-percent-skip figure is used as evidence of misplaced trust in the review signal, and the post-QA failure rate is the load-bearing proof that the gap persists when review is actually applied.
reason: The thesis is falsifiable and non-obvious as a claim, and the strongest attack does not win. The attack's best shot (that 62 percent skipping verification means review is merely too lax) is neutralized by the post-QA and post-staging failure rate, which shows defects surviving a passing gate on rated-high-quality code, separating review strictness from runtime outcome. The remaining weaknesses (unpaired percentages, single-domain vendor-survey sourcing) are source-quality concerns outside the claim-rigor mandate, not grounds for weak. Directional, actionable, and contradicts the default gate-harder reflex, so defensible.
